### Directions

|---------|---------|-----------------|-------|

| a la izquierda | to the left | | Always **a la** — feminine noun |

| detrás (de) | behind | | Requires **de** before a noun |

### Asking for and Giving Directions
| Spanish | English | Example Sentence | Notes |
|---------|---------|-----------------|-------|
| ¿Dónde está...? | Where is...? | ¿Dónde está la estación de metro? | Most basic location question. Uses **estar** (location). |
| ¿Cómo llego a...? | How do I get to...? | ¿Cómo llego al aeropuerto? | Note contraction: **a + el = al**. |
| Está a dos cuadras | It's two blocks away | | **Estar a + distance** = "to be [distance] away" |
| Queda cerca / lejos | It's nearby / far | ¿Queda lejos? — No, queda muy cerca. | **Quedar** is used for permanent locations, like estar but more natural for giving directions. |
| Siga recto | Go straight | | Usted command of **seguir**. Informal: **sigue recto**. |
| Doble a la derecha | Turn right | Doble a la derecha en la esquina. | Usted command of **doblar**. Informal: **dobla**. Also: **gire** (more formal). |

## Common Collocations
- **a dos cuadras de aquí** — two blocks from here
- **dar vuelta** — to turn (Mexico: dar vuelta a la derecha)
- **seguir derecho / seguir recto** — to keep going straight
- **tomar un taxi** — to take a taxi (not "coger" in Latin America — see False Cognates)
- **ir a pie** — to go on foot / to walk
- **ir en carro / coche** — to go by car
- **la parada del autobús** — the bus stop
- **quedar a mano derecha / izquierda** — to be on the right / left side
- **perderse** — to get lost (Me perdí = I got lost)
- **¿me puede llevar a...?** — can you take me to...? (to a taxi driver)

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **tomar** vs **coger** (to take a bus): In Spain, **coger el autobús** (to take the bus) is standard. In most of Latin America, **coger** is vulgar slang and must be avoided. Use **tomar** instead: **tomar el autobús**.
- **dirección** vs "direction": **Dirección** means both "direction" and "address." Context makes it clear: ¿Cuál es tu dirección? = What is your address?
- **esquina** vs **rincón**: Both translate to "corner." **Esquina** = outside corner (street corner). **Rincón** = inside corner (corner of a room).
- **manejar** vs **conducir**: Both mean "to drive." **Manejar** also means "to manage/handle." In Latin America, it is the standard word for driving. Spain uses **conducir** exclusively for driving.

## Dialect Variations
- **carro / coche / auto**: Mexico, Colombia, Venezuela: **carro**. Spain: **coche**. Argentina, Chile: **auto**. All are universally understood.
- **camión / autobús / colectivo / bus / micro / guagua**: The word for "bus" varies enormously. Mexico: **camión** (which elsewhere means "truck"). Argentina: **colectivo**. Chile: **micro**. Cuba/Puerto Rico/Canary Islands: **guagua** (which in other countries means "baby"). **Autobús** is understood everywhere.
- **cuadra / manzana**: Latin America uses **cuadra** for "city block." Spain uses **manzana** (which also means "apple" — context distinguishes). Both are widely understood.
- **manejar / conducir**: Latin America: **manejar**. Spain: **conducir**. Both understood in either region.
- **estacionamiento / aparcamiento / parqueadero**: Mexico: **estacionamiento**. Spain: **aparcamiento**. Colombia: **parqueadero**. All mean "parking lot."

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Address systems**: In many Latin American cities, addresses use landmarks rather than street numbers. "Dos cuadras al norte de la iglesia" (two blocks north of the church) is a real address in Costa Rica and Nicaragua. Mexico uses formal street addresses but informal directions still rely on landmarks.
- **Cuadra measurements**: A **cuadra** is not standardized. In different cities, a block can be 80-150 meters. "Está a tres cuadras" is an approximation.
- **Asking strangers for directions**: Using **usted** is appropriate. Start with **Disculpe** (excuse me, formal) before asking: **Disculpe, ¿cómo llego a...?**
- **Taxis**: In Mexico and much of Latin America, always confirm the price or ask them to use the meter (**el taxímetro**) before getting in. In some cities, you should only use registered taxis from taxi stands (**sitios**) or apps.
- **"Right" ambiguity**: **Derecho** can mean "straight ahead" or "right" depending on context and region. To avoid confusion, use **a la derecha** (to the right) and **recto** or **todo derecho** (straight ahead).

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **izquierda** — four syllables: is-KYER-da. The **zqu** cluster is unusual for English speakers. The **z** sounds like "s" in Latin America.
- **aeropuerto** — five syllables: a-e-ro-PWER-to. The **ae** at the start are two separate vowel sounds, not a diphthong.
- **autobús** — stress on the final syllable: au-to-BUS. The accent mark confirms this.
- **semáforo** — stress on the second syllable: se-MA-fo-ro. Esdrújula word (stressed on the third-to-last syllable).
- **avión** — stress on the final syllable: a-VYON. The **ió** is a diphthong — do not separate into three syllables.
- **calle** — two syllables: CA-ye (Latin America) or CA-lye (parts of Spain). The **ll** is never a silent letter.
